records.name: Kazakhstan
records.current_summary:
Kazakhstan demands real caution from trans visitors — Central Asia's most liveable country for trans people, which is a relative statement. Nothing is criminalised; legal gender recognition exists (heavily medicalised: psychiatric boards, and surgery requirements applied in practice); and revealingly, hundreds of trans people fled TO Kazakhstan from Russia after its propaganda law and LGR ban. ODIHR recorded 62 anti-LGBTI bias incidents in 2024 — real, but documented and reported, which itself indicates functioning civil society (Feminita, ECOM).

The trajectory is the concern: a “We Are Against Open and Hidden LGBT Propaganda” petition gained official review by the Ministry of Culture in 2024 (HRW urged rejection), and anti-gender MPs are vocal. Currently there is no propaganda statute, no bathroom law, and no police targeting pattern — police are unhelpful rather than predatory.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; low visibility keeps visitor exposure small; Almaty/Astana are navigable.
records.current_localsOnly: The heavily medicalised LGR process (psychiatric boards, surgery requirements) is resident-facing; the propaganda petition and anti-gender MPs are trajectory signals affecting residents.
records.current_outOfScope: LGR medicalisation and the propaganda petition are resident-facing/trajectory signals.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review covering Jan–Dec 2023 (Kazakhstan): documents access-to-services bias (an LGBTQI+ education NGO denied employment-site registration after listing its focus), bias-motivated violence (an LGBTQI activist almost run over with no investigation), and a wave of transgender people arriving from Russia since 2022.

OSCE/ODIHR Hate Crime Reporting 2024 summary for Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan has not reported hate-crime data to ODIHR since the 2018 report, has no nominated National Point of Contact for hate crimes, and would benefit from victim-support and awareness measures — an institutional-gap finding on documentation of bias violence.

HRW (10 Jul 2024): in June 2024 the Ministry of Culture and Information said it was reviewing a 'We Are against Open and Hidden LGBT Propaganda in Kazakhstan!' petition (Union of Parents) that met the threshold for government consideration; HRW warns the proposed ban would violate rights nationwide — a live, dated legislative threat.

ECOM regional report library page (2024): ECOM has monitored and documented rights violations against LGBT people since 2017; the analysis identifies health-right barriers across the EECA region as a whole and in individual countries (incl. Kazakhstan), plus informal behavioural practices missed by policy analysis — abstract-level, country data is in the linked report body.

HRW (24 Sep 2019): Kazakhstan's Supreme Court ordered compensation from a Facebook user who posted a video of two women kissing and solicited homophobic comments — privacy rights upheld over a 'moral foundations' defence; the women fled Kazakhstan for eight months fearing for safety, illustrating both the privacy remedy and the social risk.

records.name: Nicaragua
records.current_summary: Nicaragua demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans (sodomy was decriminalised in 2008), but NGOs document 108 cases of violence against the LGTBIQ+ community in 2024 alone, and 10 murders of trans women in the last two and a half years. Since 2018 the Ortega regime has shut down or exiled virtually all independent civil society — including LGBT organisations — so there is no domestic protection infrastructure and no recourse; arbitrary detention is used broadly against perceived opponents.
records.current_localsOnly: The 108-case violence count and 10 trans-women murders fall on residents; the civil-society shutdown affects resident organisations.
records.current_outOfScope: Generalised repression affects all; the trans-murder count is trans-specific.

sources.claim: thin: no usable finding

US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report on Nicaragua: documents a police/parapolice campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against perceived regime enemies that authorities did not investigate or prosecute, and lists violence or threats against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex persons among significant violations. For this record: official US assessment that anti-LGBTI abuse occurs inside a climate of state impunity.

Amnesty International (May 2019): the post-April-2018 protest crackdown left at least 325 dead and more than 2,000 injured per the IACHR; journalist Miguel Mora describes being beaten by a pro-government mob and being targeted partly for being gay, illustrating the intersection of political repression and homophobia. For this record: documented violence context and homophobia within the repression, with the casualty figures.

PinkNews (Nov 2007): Nicaragua's new penal code, effective March 2008, repealed the 1992 sodomy law (1-3 years' imprisonment), whose vague wording had also been usable against LGBT-rights campaigning and sexual-health work. For this record: dated decriminalisation — same-sex conduct not criminalised since 2008.

records.name: Suriname
records.current_summary:
Suriname demands real caution from trans visitors — legally unremarkable, socially mixed. Same-sex conduct is legal; the constitution's “any other status” clause is read to cover SOGI discrimination; and the 2022 Equal Treatment Labour Act added employment protections. There is no legal gender recognition and no documented trans-murder pattern, but Paramaribo's small community reports routine harassment, and the interior has essentially no protection.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; modest street risk in Paramaribo; low tourist infrastructure generally.
records.current_localsOnly: No LGR — resident-facing; the 2022 labour act and the harassment reports concern residents.
records.current_outOfScope: LGR absence and interior governance gaps are resident-facing.

sources.claim: Country overview updated 12 Mar 2026: same-sex relations legal for men and women nationwide; legal gender recognition NOT possible; LGBTI organisations CAN register. Constitution Article 8.2's 'any other status' clause is read by the government as extending to sexual orientation and gender identity despite no explicit statutory protection.

Civil-society report of July 2024 (Projekta Foundation with VIDS and LGBT Platform): Constitution Article 8 covers SOGI only implicitly through 'any other status', and same-sex conduct has not been criminalised since 1869. The LGBT Platform Suriname, founded 29 August 2011, unites PAREA, New Monday Foundation, Suriname Men United, Women's Way and Trans in Action; the report urges a comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation, gender identity and disability.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Suriname: documents the Bouterse trial, police brutality, corruption, and 'discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and intersex (LGBTI) persons and other minorities'.

Submission to the UN Human Rights Committee (115th session) from LGBT Platform Suriname, Heartland Alliance and Akahata: despite constitutional protection LGBTI persons still face daily discrimination, violence and stigmatization. It records that in March 2015 Penal Code Articles 175, 175a and 176 were revised to cover discrimination and hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation.

Human Rights Committee review of Suriname, July 2024: the State asserted its laws protect against discrimination including on sexual orientation, backed by monitoring bodies such as the National Inclusive Labour Market Commission, while experts pressed on implementing the Inter-American Court's judgment on transgender identity. The Committee welcomed abolition of the death penalty in the Penal Code (2015) and Military Code (2021).

UN UPR pre-session summary of March 2016 from the Suriname LGBT Platform: since the 2011 UPR the State revised the penal code to equalise the age of consent for same- and opposite-sex conduct and to add sexual-orientation discrimination provisions. The platform also reports it has been excluded from state consultative processes despite repeated requests.

records.name: Kyrgyzstan
records.current_summary:
Kyrgyzstan is dangerous for trans visitors — once Central Asia's relative haven, now regressing. In 2023-2024 Kyrgyzstan adopted two discriminatory laws targeting the LGBTI community and restricting LGBTI organisations, accompanied by homophobic/transphobic MP rhetoric; TGEU records Kyrgyzstan (2021) among the countries that removed legal gender recognition entirely (the 2020 Civil Status Acts law blocks birth-certificate changes). Same-sex conduct is legal (1998), but police abuse and extortion of LGBT people are documented, and the community (Kyrgyz Indigo) operates under pressure.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but LGR removal + police extortion culture + active anti-LGBT political campaign make outing risky.
records.current_localsOnly: The 2020 law blocking birth-certificate changes (LGR removal) is resident-facing; the NGO-restriction laws affect resident organisations.
records.current_outOfScope: LGR removal is resident-facing; NGO-restriction laws signal the enforcement climate.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (Kyrgyzstan): anti-LGBT legislative pushes accompanied by a media campaign of homophobic and transphobic statements from MPs; since 2021 trans people cannot obtain legal recognition (Law on Civil Acts amendments); ECOM data shows high stigma and discrimination, particularly from law enforcement.

TGEU Trans Rights Index Map 2024: Kyrgyzstan (2021) joined Hungary, Bulgaria and Russia in removing the right to legal gender recognition; for Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan the 'bare minimum' of not banning recognition is all they score — the regional floor on trans legal status.

OutRight International Kyrgyzstan profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): consensual same-sex activity decriminalised 1998 with age of consent equal at 16; no same-sex marriage or civil unions and a 2016 constitutional amendment explicitly bans same-sex marriage; the provision allowing trans people to change legal gender markers was removed by a 2020 amendment to the Law on Civil Status.

ECOM study (2024) on trans people's access to medical services including HIV prevention and HRT across the EECA region (with country coordinators for Georgia, Armenia, Ukraine, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Moldova, Kyrgyzstan, Azerbaijan, Tajikistan) - includes information for trans migrants.
thin: no usable finding

RFE/RL feature on the closure of Bishkek's lone LGBT club (Asanbay car-wash venue): patrons entered furtively through a derelict yard as the atmosphere worsened — documentary evidence of public LGBT life contracting in the capital; no other gay venue remained.

The Guardian (19 Oct 2017): why Bishkek's only gay club closed — the Kyrgyz capital had been a relatively safe haven and liberal beacon in Central Asia until a ban on 'LGBT propaganda'; patrons said 'all of us will be victims at some point', documenting the closing of organised gay nightlife.

records.name: Tajikistan
records.current_summary:
Tajikistan is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but police conducted a series of raids against LGBTIQ people in several cities in 2022-2023, and documentation (IPHR 2024) shows systematic patterns: discrimination in all spheres, police abuse, arbitrary detention, and forced disclosure. There is no transparent legal gender recognition (a medicalised registration route exists on paper under the Civil Status Acts law), no anti-discrimination protection, and authorities have previously maintained informal registries of LGBT citizens.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but police raids + registry practices + zero recourse make discovery dangerous.
records.current_localsOnly: The informal LGBT registries and the on-paper medicalised LGR route are resident-facing; the raid pattern primarily targets residents but defines the enforcement climate for any discovered trans person.
records.current_outOfScope: Registry practices and raid patterns target residents but define the enforcement climate for any discovered trans person.

sources.claim: IPHR report 'Rights for All?' (Feb 2024): consensual same-sex relations decriminalised since 1998, yet authorities introduced a police register of LGBTIQ people in 2016; 2022/2023 police raids brought forced HIV-testing and arbitrary criminal charges; ill-treatment, sexual abuse and extortion by police documented; the 2022 anti-discrimination law fails to address discrimination — the systematic-risk evidence for a visitor.

Outright International overview (updated Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal throughout the country since independence, no SOGI non-discrimination protection; in 2024 ECOM recorded 27 human-rights violation cases against LGBT people with police arbitrary arrests, blackmail and extortion; a 2017 government registry of 'proven' LGBT persons flagged — legality without safety.

ECOM study (2024) on trans people's access to medical services incl. HIV prevention/treatment and HRT across the EECA region, with a Tajikistan country coordinator contributing — maps what gender-affirming/HIV care is actually reachable in-country and includes guidance for trans migrants.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024): police lure LGBT people into fake meetings to register them in a database, harvest social-media contacts and extort money (10+ cases in Sughd); forced/sham marriages used against LGBT people with police inaction; the 2022 anti-discrimination law only partially aligns with UN standards — quantified police-entrapment risk.

ECOM legislative analysis (2020): comparative analysis identifying legal barriers and gaps for gay men, MSM and trans people in Tajikistan, built from a questionnaire completed by local partners — documents where the written law protects but practice does not.

HRW World Report 2017, Tajikistan chapter: the human-rights situation deteriorated sharply in 2016 — opposition leadership sentenced, human-rights lawyers imprisoned, and a predetermined referendum extending presidential rule — the repressive state context surrounding LGBT life.

Global Voices (Jan 20, 2013): despite decriminalisation 15 years earlier (1998) there is very little tolerance; those who disclose orientation become targets of physical and psychological abuse including from police, and the community remains one of the most closed in society — social-climate evidence predating the 2016 registry.

records.name: Laos
records.current_summary: Laos demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, and Laos has a socially visible tradition of trans feminine people; but there is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, no registered LGBT organisation (the one-party state restricts all civil society), and no documented recourse. Vientiane and Luang Prabang are accustomed to tourists; the risk is administrative (an opaque state) more than violent.
records.current_localsOnly: No LGR and no registered LGBT organisations — resident-facing gaps.
records.current_outOfScope: Civil-society restrictions affect all; no trans-specific mechanism documented.

sources.claim: thin: no usable finding
thin: no usable finding

Human Dignity Trust history: Laos (with Cambodia) achieved independence from France in the 1950s and modelled its penal code on the French system — it has never formally criminalised same-sex conduct, distinguishing it from neighbours that retained colonial sodomy offences.

GlobalGayz first-person account (2000, Richard Ammon): during a week in Vientiane the writer met a small circle of lesbians and gay men whose lives centred on a few restaurants and friendship networks — the country's LGBT scene is small, discreet and social rather than public or institutional.

Al Jazeera in-depth (Oct 2018): government crackdown on social media — influential Facebook users ('net idols') face retribution for posts, and 'Proud to be us Laos', the country's only LGBT advocacy group, is quoted; indicates online LGBT expression operates under tightening state attention.

EEAS page (title-verified; body behind JavaScript wall): the EU celebrated International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia in Vientiane — diplomatic visibility for LGBT rights; no further detail retrievable.

records.name: Timor-Leste
records.current_summary: Timor-Leste is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, the constitution's equality provisions have been read inclusively, and Dili hosts an annual Pride march with government participation — remarkable for a young, Catholic-majority nation. There is no legal gender recognition and services are thin, but there is no documented pattern of police targeting or anti-trans violence, and the small community (CODIVA, Arco Iris) operates openly.
records.current_outOfScope: Service thinness and LGR absence are resident-facing.

sources.claim: Australian Volunteers Program Pride Guide, Timor-Leste: country snapshot for volunteers — same-sex sexual acts decriminalised in 1975; the UN Human Rights Council joint statement on SOGI was adopted in 2011; Timor-Leste voted in favour of the 2013 UN resolution on vulnerability/disability... sets out the legal and policy context for living openly as a volunteer.

New Naratif (June 2018): Timor-Leste's first-ever Pride parade in 2017 drew international attention and a televised endorsement from the Prime Minister, while the report also captures day-to-day rejection (the organiser's family messages) — social-climate depth beyond the headline acceptance.

VOA (July 2018): East Timor held its second annual LGBT pride parade in Dili on July 20, cementing a regional leadership role while neighbours Indonesia and Malaysia turn hostile — the open-environment evidence for visitors.

Star Observer (July 2019): an estimated 3,000 people joined the 'Marsa Diversidade' Pride March in Dili on July 12 — six times the turnout of the 2017 first parade; President Francisco Guterres publicly backed the event ('I am a President for all people'). Quantified growth of visible acceptance.

records.name: Côte d'Ivoire
records.current_summary:
Côte d'Ivoire is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp recent deterioration. Long considered West Africa's tolerant outlier (same-sex conduct has never been criminalised), the country saw a wave of violence in late 2024: social-media influencers exhorted followers to “hunt” gay and gender-nonconforming people, and dozens of assaults and beatings followed (NYT, Oct 2024). There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection; police response to the hunt wave was inadequate.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but the 2024 hunt-down campaign makes visible gender nonconformity dangerous, especially in Abidjan.
records.current_outOfScope: The 2024 violence wave targeted perceived gay men primarily but gender-nonconforming people are the most visible targets.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying NYT article (Oct 2024) covers the situation of LGBTQ people in Ivory Coast (Côte d'Ivoire).

UNDP report (Dec 2024) 'African Commission Resolution 275: Ten Years of Advancing LGBT+ Rights in Africa' - includes a Côte d'Ivoire country overview assessing the protective legal environment, investigation/prosecution of perpetrators, access to justice, civic space, and inclusion of LGBT+ people.

US State Department 2023 report, Côte d'Ivoire: same-sex conduct not criminalised, but LGBTQI+ persons faced violence — three community deaths reported in the year; police responses to non-state violence were sometimes slow and ineffective and often blamed the victim; a transgender man was beaten in Abobo, Abidjan, while walking with another man. Authorities were handling complaints somewhat better than in previous years.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Côte d'Ivoire: post-electoral-crisis context (3,000 deaths, sexual violence, displacement) - general human-rights baseline with limited LGBT-specific content.

Critical African Studies (2015), Thomann & Corey-Boulet, 'Violence, Exclusion and Resilience among Ivoirian Travestis': travestis (born anatomically male, living as women) face harsher stigmatization and violence than sexual minorities whose gender normativity avoids attention, and have been underserved by Ivoirian rights groups that distanced themselves from them; examines isolation after the 2010-11 post-election violence.

Same article via PMC canonical URL (Thomann & Corey-Boulet 2015): the key academic source on trans-feminine people's experiences in Côte d'Ivoire — documented violence and social exclusion of travestis alongside their resilience; duplicate of the ncbi copy retained as canonical mirror.

freshness_all.fact: Current overview describes same-sex activity as legal for both sexes (no specific protections, unrecognised unions); the 'acts against nature'/public-indecency provisions in the cited 2023-era reports no longer appear — recheck criminalisation claims.
